title: atlas-graph tests — the laws that keep the graph honest

overview.l1: This folder is the project's proof pile. Each file checks one promise about the Bible graph: that the file the server actually loads (data/compiled/graph.bin) matches what building it from scratch would produce, that rebuilding it twice gives byte-identical results, that every relationship (a verse belongs to a chapter, an event has a date, a fact names its source) is really backed by real data and not a decoration, and that dozens of specific, owner-reported bugs stay fixed. If one of these tests goes red, something the app shows you — a verse, a date, a map border, an attribution — would be silently wrong or missing.
overview.l2: Every *.rs file here is its own Rust 'integration test' crate: Cargo compiles each one as a separate binary that links against atlas-graph and its sibling crates (atlas-core, atlas-etl, graph-types) purely through their public APIs, the same way an outside consumer would. Each file lists one or more `#[test] fn` — a function `cargo test` discovers and runs, reporting pass/fail from its `assert!`/`assert_eq!` calls. Almost every file reads the project's own real, committed data (`data/raw`, `data/curated`, sometimes the shipped `data/compiled/graph.bin` itself) rather than a synthetic fixture, because these are supposed to be true statements about the actual Bible Atlas, not about a toy example. Building that real data is expensive, so most files cache it once per test binary with `std::sync::OnceLock` (Rust's 'compute this exactly once, safely, even if multiple tests ask for it' primitive) instead of paying the cost per test.
overview.l3: These are `tests/*.rs` integration tests for the `atlas-graph` crate (Cargo convention: anything under `tests/` compiles as an independent crate per file, sees only `pub` items, and runs via `cargo test -p atlas-graph`). Most files duplicate a small `real_atlas_data()`/`real_graph()` helper rather than sharing one (a deliberate crate convention, noted in several files' own headers) so each file's real-data construction is self-contained and auditable. Two files load the actual shipped artifact instead of rebuilding (`kjv_case_artifact_real_data.rs`, `provenance_registry_real_data.rs`) because their claim is specifically about what ships, not what a fresh build would produce. Disclosed costs and ceilings are load-bearing: `artifact_conformance.rs`'s 4-second load ceiling was retargeted after a documented flake under parallel `cargo test --workspace` runs; `determinism.rs` discloses its own two-independent-full-build cost at ~90 seconds and calls itself 'this crate's single most expensive test'. Several files pin exact real-data counts as named constants (e.g. `version_root_regression.rs`'s `EXPECTED_VERSION_HEX`, `attestation_exclusivity_real_data.rs`'s `SWEEP_*_PAIRS`) with the rule that a deliberate content change updates the constant in the same commit, never silently.

files.role: Proves the compiled graph.bin loads fast and answers identically to a fresh build.
files.l1: Every so often the Bible Atlas's whole dataset gets compiled once into a single file. This test proves two promises about that file: the server can load it in well under 4 seconds (so it starts up fast), and once loaded, it answers every question — a verse's text, an event's connections — exactly the same as building the graph fresh from the raw sources would. If this broke, the shipped file could quietly disagree with the truth, or startup could stall.
files.l2: This integration test builds the graph twice: once the normal way (`atlas_graph::build`, 'implementation #1'), and once by dumping that graph to bytes (`artifact::dump`), writing them to a temp file, and reading them back (`artifact::read_file` + `to_service_parts`, 'implementation #2'). A `OnceLock` caches the expensive real-data compile so both `#[test]` functions in the file share one build instead of paying for it twice. `std::time::Instant` times only the load step, compared against a named `LOAD_CEILING` constant. The key assertion, `atlas_graph_types::store::assert_answers_match`, is the crate's 'two implementations must agree' law: it walks the shared `GraphQuery` trait's methods on both graphs and compares every answer. A second test builds a `GraphService` (the production-facing wrapper) both `from_sources` and `from_artifact` and checks their `version()` and rendered verse text agree.
files.l3: `serialized_artifact_is_admitted_and_loads_under_the_committed_ceiling` (line 101) builds via `atlas_graph::build::build_graph_from_sources_with_eras_and_brainfuel_and_concord_and_kretzmann`, dumps+writes+reads, times only `read_file`+`to_service_parts`+`build_indexes`+`add_justified_by` against `LOAD_CEILING = 4s` (line 44), then runs `store::assert_answers_match` (untimed admission pass) and `law_check::indexes_derive_exactly_from_rows` over the FROM-ARTIFACT graph specifically. `graph_service_from_artifact_serves_the_same_answers_as_from_sources` (line 204) compares `GraphService::from_sources_with_eras_and_brainfuel_and_concord_and_kretzmann` against `::from_artifact` by `version()` and `window::render` on John 3:16. Disclosed caveat (lines 18-43): the ceiling moved from a flat 3s to 4s after a documented flake under parallel `cargo test --workspace` load (4/4 in-suite failures at 3.51-4.16s vs. 4/4 passes isolated at 2.58-2.76s); parallelizing `Graph::build_indexes` lowered real numbers to 2.39-2.59s even under two concurrent full-workspace test runs, leaving a ~54% margin, not a knife-edge one.

files.role: Pins the owner-reported Attests-vs-Mentions/Analogue corrections over real data.
files.l1: The owner found a real bug: some Bible passages were marked as *narrating* an event when they only *mention* it in passing, and two similar-but-different Gospel stories (two healed lepers) were wrongly tied together as one. This file proves those exact mistakes are fixed and stay fixed, and it counts the whole backlog of similar suspicious cases so it can't quietly grow or shrink without someone noticing.
files.l2: Builds the real graph once (`real_graph`, `OnceLock`-cached) via `atlas_graph::build::build_graph_from_sources_with_eras`, then filters its row tables (`graph.attests`, `graph.mentions`, `graph.analogue`) with iterator adapters (`.filter()`, `.map()`, `.collect()`) and Rust's `matches!` macro for pattern-matching an enum variant (`MentionedEntity::Event`). Two tests check the owner's exact two named cases end to end (the espousal of Mary keeps both its facts, just retyped; the two leper healings stay distinct events joined by an `Analogue` row). A third test calls the crate's own standing law functions (`law_check::attestation_is_exclusive` and friends) directly against the real corpus. A fourth pins the size and shape of the whole curation backlog (`attestation_pending::PENDING`) as named constants, so a future change to the queue must update the constants in the same commit rather than drift silently.
files.l3: `the_espousal_of_mary_is_mention_only_and_keeps_both_facts` (line 61) asserts `graph.attests` has zero rows for `theo-249` and exactly two `Mentions` rows (MAT.1.18, LUK.1.27) — both halves asserted together because either alone would pass on a broken (data-loss) shape. `the_two_leprosy_events_are_distinct_and_joined_by_an_analogue` (line 112) proves `mat_leper_healed` keeps its own MAT.8.1-4 span and `rob_leper_healed` never attests it, joined instead by a `graph.analogue` row. `the_attestation_laws_hold_over_the_real_corpus` (line 161) calls `atlas_graph::law_check::{attestation_is_exclusive, attestation_inventory_has_no_stale_rows, analogue_rows_join_two_distinct_events}` — the same functions `pipeline::LawCheckPass` runs on every build, re-asserted here as named tests. `the_corpus_sweep_totals_are_pinned` (line 184) checks `attestation_pending::PENDING` sorts/dedups cleanly and pins its size via named constants `SWEEP_PENDING_PAIRS = 824`, `SWEEP_CONTAINMENT_PAIRS = 590`, `SWEEP_OVERLAP_PAIRS = 234` (lines 243-245), and asserts three specific pairs are absent (resolved).

files.role: Proves books and chapters are real, correctly-shaped container nodes with declared rows.
files.l1: Chapters and books aren't magic labels in this app — they're real nodes in the graph, the same kind of thing a place or a person is, connected by real 'contains' and 'comes before/after' relationships. This file counts them (66 books, 1,189 chapters, 31,102 verses) and walks those relationships the way the reader UI would: a chapter's verses, a book's chapters, and 'next/previous chapter' navigation across book boundaries (Genesis 50 leads into Exodus 1).
files.l2: Uses the shared `real_graph()` pattern this crate repeats per file, then queries the graph exactly the way a client would: through `PositionRef(...).edges(g, &EdgeQuery { kind, cursor, limit })`, the generic edge-traversal port every relation in the app rides (not a direct field read). `EdgeKind::Directed(RelationId::Contains, Direction::Forward)` and its siblings are Rust `const`s built from an `enum`, used as lookup keys. A small local `edges()` helper wraps pagination into a flat `Vec<Position>` for easy `assert_eq!`. Two tests are 'standing gate' laws also run at build time: `container_containment_is_a_forest` (no cycles, one parent each) and `indexes_derive_exactly_from_rows` (the served indexes are a pure function of the declared row tables, never hand-patched afterward).
files.l3: `the_real_canon_declares_every_container_row` (line 87) counts book/chapter `Container` nodes (66/1,189) and `graph.contains_bible` rows split by `ContainerContent::{Loci, Container}` variant (1,189 Loci rows covering 31,102 verse loci; 1,189 book⊃chapter rows; 2,378 total) plus 1,253 `canon_succession` rows (1,188 chapter steps + 65 book steps). `container_containment_is_a_forest_over_the_real_canon` (127) and `served_indexes_are_a_pure_function_of_the_declared_rows` (139) call `atlas_graph::law_check::{container_containment_is_a_forest, indexes_derive_exactly_from_rows}` directly. `chapter_succession_navigates_within_and_across_book_boundaries` (200) asserts the disclosed boundary choice explicitly: GEN.50→EXO.1 and MAL.4→MAT.1 (the testament seam) follow canon order with no special case, and honest ends (GEN.1 has no predecessor, REV.22 no successor) return empty, not a placeholder.

files.l1: The app shows a verse's text in the KJV, but behind the scenes it also lines that verse up against five other historic Bible editions (Latin, Hebrew, French Douay-Rheims, Swedish, Greek). This short test proves that merge actually worked over the real vendored files: every one of the roughly 147,000 (edition, verse) pairs found a home, none were orphaned, and exactly six extra 'translation' entries were created.
files.l2: Calls the adapter function under test, `brainfuel_adapter::normalize`, directly against a minimal, real-but-partial `BuildCtx` (built with `pipeline::BuildCtx::with_eras_and_brainfuel`) rather than running the whole six-stage ETL pipeline — cheaper, because `normalize` only reads `ctx.graph.nodes` (already built by `kjv_adapter::normalize`, called first) and `ctx.brainfuel`. files.role: Re-proves the four dating-consistency laws (E1-E4) computed straight off graph rows.
files.l1: Every dated event in the Bible Atlas (creation, the Exodus, David's reign...) has to agree with a table of well-known anchor dates and with the books that actually narrate it. This file re-checks that agreement, but reading the dates straight out of the graph's own edges rather than a separate summary table — proving the graph itself, not just an old side-calculation, gets the chronology right.
files.l2: Builds the real graph and, independently, a `HashMap<String, ResolvedPlacement>` by walking every `graph.dated_by` row through `event_world::resolve_timepoint` (never trusting a cached year field). `HashMap`/`HashSet` are Rust's hash-keyed collections (unordered, fast lookup by key — used here to index events and books by id). Four `#[test]` functions named `e1_`..`e4_` mirror four laws already proven elsewhere over the older `AtlasData`-shaped data, restated here against the graph's `Attests` rows and `atlas_graph_types::chrono::temporal_order`. A fifth test is a single named regression: a specific event's date must resolve to the historically corrected year, not the raw import's anachronistic one.
files.l3: `build_real()` (line 66) builds `RealGraph { atlas, graph, resolved }` where `resolved` re-derives every `dated_by` row's placement via `event_world::resolve_timepoint`, paired with `chrono.resolved[&id].seq`. `graph_witness_books` (97) reads witness books from `graph.attests` rows directly (not `Event.verses`), applying the same `is_recounting`/`is_exempted` exclusion the production window check uses. `e1_every_bound_anchor_equals_its_graphs_own_resolved_event_year` (125) requires exactly 4 typed deferrals (`ANCHOR_DEFERRALS`) and zero unexplained mismatches. `e3_...monotone_under_the_graphs_own_temporal_order` (184) sorts bound anchors by table year and checks `temporal_order` agrees, tie only where table years match. `e4_...era_boundary_anchors...` (219) checks every dated event's witness-book windows land strictly before/after every `era_boundary` anchor, with a straddle carve-out. `theo_87_nimrods_kingdom_resolves_to_the_corrected_traditional_year` (290) pins `theo-87` to `-2242` (Ussher), guarding against the raw Theographic import's `-1822`.

files.role: Proves the compiled artifact's bytes are identical across two independent builds.
files.l1: If you build the atlas's data file twice from the exact same sources, you should get the exact same bytes — not just the same meaning, the same bytes, in the same order. This test proves that, closing off an old bug class where computer-internal 'random-order' data structures made every build slightly different even though nothing had really changed.
files.l2: Calls its own `real_sources()` helper TWICE, independently (not once with the result reused), so the test proves the whole ETL pipeline is deterministic, not just the graph-build half over an already-fixed input. `build_and_encode` runs the exact sequence `atlas-graph-compile` performs (build → dump → `artifact::encode`) and returns `Vec<u8>`, compared byte-for-byte with `assert_eq!`.
files.l3: `serialized_artifact_bytes_are_deterministic_across_independent_builds` (95) sanity-checks the raw source strings match between the two independent reads, then asserts `bytes_a.len() == bytes_b.len()` and `bytes_a == bytes_b`. Disclosed cost (lines 31-49): builds the ~344k-cross-reference-edge graph twice, including all six brain-fuel editions each time — measured directly at 89.70s and 89.79s standalone, 92.60s inside a full `cargo test --workspace` run; the file calls itself 'this crate's single most expensive test' and flags that a slower CI machine could plausibly cross a notional 90s budget, a disclosed-but-accepted tradeoff rather than a silently re-budgeted one.

files.role: Checks the C2C3 map-facing exports (gazetteer/chronology JSON) for drift, resolution, and a documented hash gap.
files.l1: The map system consumes exported JSON files (a gazetteer of places, a list of dated events) rather than the graph directly. This file proves those exports stay honest: every dated event actually resolves to a real year (none silently dropped), a few named places the map system depends on are findable by their expected names, every time-span has a sensible start before its end, and the exports round-trip through JSON without losing data. It also documents, on purpose, one known gap: the embedded version stamp doesn't change if only a date's resolved value changes.
files.l2: Builds everything once per test binary into a `Built` struct (cached via `OnceLock`, `#[derive(Clone)]` so each test gets its own cheap copy of small owned data) rather than each test paying for a real compile again. `MemStore::default().publish(graph)` is the in-memory `GraphPublisher` implementation that stamps a content-hash `GraphVersion`; `version_hex` renders it as a hex string for comparison. The final test mutates a *copy* of a `Chronology` derivation (never the graph itself) to prove, mechanically rather than by assertion in prose, that the exported `atlas_version_root` field does not change even though the exported content genuinely differs.

files.role: The largest test file in the crate: real-data timeline-ordering laws, duplicate-event rectification, and a five-part global-chronology property audit.
files.l1: This is the biggest single collection of chronology bug-fixes in the app, all proven against the real, full timeline of dated events. It checks: there are hundreds of real dated events; the very first (Creation) and very last events make sense; three sets of duplicate events (the same story imported twice under different ids) are properly merged; Jesus's baptism sorts before his temptation; a whole-Bible audit that every event's chronological order agrees with its reading order (with every disclosed exception explained by name); the whole Gospel account sorts before Acts; and several owner-reported date mistakes (like Solomon's dream being wrongly dated to Saul's era) are fixed and stay fixed.
files.l2: This file was mechanically relocated from `atlas-core/src/narrative.rs`'s own test module (its own header explains why: a dev-dependency cycle prevented keeping it in atlas-core once the real-data source moved to atlas-etl). It uses `atlas_core::narrative::global_timeline_position` and `atlas_core::data::AtlasData` almost exclusively — this is really an atlas-core-level test that lives here purely to break a crate-dependency cycle. Its style is heavy with `HashMap`/`BTreeSet` bookkeeping and closures (e.g. a big `is_justified` closure enumerating every accepted class of 'reading order disagrees with chronological order' case, each with its own paragraph of reasoning) rather than typed graph queries, since it predates the graph-based rewrite.

files.l1: Older parts of the app still expect data shaped the old way (a flat list of events, places, narratives) rather than graph rows. A translation layer rebuilds that old shape from the new graph. This test proves that translation is complete and correct for every single item, not just the handful any one spot-check test happens to name — every real event, place, narrative, and verse reconstructs field-for-field identical to a fresh from-scratch build.
files.l2: Compares two independently-built things: the OLD/reference side is a fresh `atlas_etl::compile::compile` (never touching the graph at all), and the NEW/under-test side is `atlas_graph::legacy::atlas_data_overlay` fed by `GraphService::from_artifact` loading the real committed `data/compiled/graph.bin` — the exact production sequence `atlas-server`'s default startup path runs. Since `Event`/`Place`/`Narrative` already `derive(PartialEq, Debug)`, each test is a sorted-by-id `assert_eq!` over the whole collection — no new test infrastructure needed, which the file's own header notes as the code review's 'right-sized' judgment.

files.role: Checks PeopleGroup node identity, reclassification, and eponym (named-after) rows over real data.
files.l1: Some entities in the atlas are peoples/nations (Ammonites, Jebusites) rather than individual persons — and a few used to be miscategorized as a single 'person' when they're really a people group. This file proves that reclassification landed correctly and exhaustively (38 real PeopleGroup nodes from three sources, nine of them switched over from Person), that mentions of these groups carry the right sense, that every 'named after' claim (a nation named after its ancestor) cites real Scripture, and it honestly reports exactly which descriptions did and didn't fill in from Easton's dictionary.
files.l2: Runs the pipeline directly for `ctx.graph` access, the same shape `description_real_data.rs` uses. Filters `ctx.graph.nodes` by `NodeKind::PeopleGroup`/`NodeKind::Person` to count node kinds, and filters `ctx.graph.mentions` by matching the `MentionedEntity` enum's `PeopleGroup`/`Person` variants to check which 'sense' a mention carries. Several tests pin an exact roster (a `Vec<&str>`, sorted, `assert_eq!`'d against a computed list) rather than just a count, so a regression in either direction — gaining or losing a match — is caught and named, not just counted.
files.l3: `peoplegroup_node_counts_match_all_three_sources_exactly` (55) pins `atlas.people_groups.len() == 23`, `people_group_seeds.len() == 6`, `people_group_reclassify.len() == 9`, and the built graph's `PeopleGroup` node count at exactly 38, with each reclassified slug's `Person` node confirmed gone and its `PeopleGroup` node confirmed present under the same raw id. `reclassified_mention_rows_carry_peoplegroup_sense_at_a_real_locus` (91) spot-checks `jebusite_748` carries exactly its two real Theographic `verse_links` (GEN.10.16, 1CH.1.14) as PeopleGroup-sense mentions, explicitly NOT fabricating a JOS.15.63 row the source doesn't attest. `every_named_after_row_is_scripture_grounded_and_the_seed_counts_match_decision_3` (130) pins 18 curated rows, calls `peoples_adapter::every_named_after_row_has_a_scripture_ground`, and spot-checks Ammonites (single ground) vs. Edomites (two real grounds). `group_description_fill_matches_the_exact_disclosed_roster` (225) pins the exact 8-of-38 filled roster by name (Arkite, Canaanites, Pharisees, Philistines, Sadducees, Scribes, Sinite, Zemarite), explicitly disclosing which groups do NOT fill (plural curated labels vs. Easton's singular headwords) rather than silently patching a fuzzy match. `pg1b_real_data_yields_exactly_13_mentions_rows_at_the_reported_loci` (263) pins Tribe of Judah's one real verse as PRO.25.1 (explicitly NOT JDG.1.2, correcting a plausible-but-wrong assumption) and Nation of Israel's 12 Psalms verses, exact.

files.role: The resolution law: every piece of data in the real artifact must resolve to a named source in the registry.
files.l1: The owner's rule is simple: every piece of data must say where it came from. This file is that rule enforced as code: it scans the real shipped file for every distinct 'this came from X' tag and checks each one is registered with a real source name — never blank, never ambiguous, and never a registered source that nothing actually uses. It also guards against a new kind of data quietly slipping past this check in the future.
files.l2: Unlike almost every other file in this crate, `real_graph()` loads the actual committed `data/compiled/graph.bin` (via `artifact::read_file` + `to_service_parts`) rather than rebuilding from raw sources — because the from-sources builder used elsewhere only covers KJV + cross-references, missing five whole provenance kinds (Concord, Kretzmann, red-letter, brainfuel, sc-overlap) the shipped artifact carries. A `macro_rules! sweep!` macro (Rust's pattern-based code-generation facility) expands into one line per provenance-bearing `Graph` field, avoiding 20 near-identical hand-written lines. `BTreeMap`/`BTreeSet` (sorted collections) keep the output deterministic for comparison.
files.l3: `provenance_by_family` (63) sweeps every `pub provenance:`-bearing row family (via the `sweep!` macro) plus `nodes`, keyed by field name. `every_distinct_provenance_id_in_the_artifact_resolves_to_a_registry_source` (125) is the law itself: every distinct provenance *kind* (via `atlas_core::sources::split_provenance_id`) must resolve to exactly one `[[provenance]]` registry row whose own `source` exists — reporting unresolved/dangling/duplicated separately. `every_declared_provenance_row_is_inhabited_by_the_real_artifact` (162) is the mirror direction: no dead registry rows. `the_sweep_covers_every_provenance_bearing_row_family` (228) is a completeness guard that counts `pub provenance:` field declarations across all of `graph-types/src` by reading the directory (fix round 1: previously named three files by hand, silently missing any new file) and reconciles the count against the swept families by an explicit equation (22 fields − 2 node.rs non-row fields = 20 row structs + 1 second Contains vector + 1 nodes map = 22 families). `the_runtime_index_and_the_test_sweep_name_exactly_the_same_families` (287) reconciles this file's own sweep against `atlas_graph::provenance::ProvenanceIndex::build`'s runtime family list, closing a drift hole a prior review found. Two more tests PIN, by identity, the full 26-kind provenance inventory (`PINNED_INVENTORY`, 331) and the complete per-family provenance map (`PINNED_FAMILIES`, 405) — the latter's own doc comment discloses the batch's own authoring mistake (assuming `attests` was multi-sourced when it isn't) as the reason the fact is code now, not prose.

files.role: Pins real SpokenAt coverage (461/470) and honestly categorizes the 9 uncovered ranges as data gaps, not code bugs.
files.l1: Jesus's recorded words ('red-letter' text) are also linked to where he was standing when he said them, when that's known. This file pins how well that linkage works over the real data (461 of 470 speech ranges, 98.1%) and, for the 9 that don't connect, proves each one is a genuine gap in the source location data — not something the code could fix by trying harder.
files.l2: Builds the real graph with red-letter data included (aligned against KJV-case-restored verses, matching what the real build does internally). The key data structure is a `BTreeMap<String, ((u8,u16,u16),(u8,u16,u16))>` tracking each event's own reconstructed min/max verse span — read from real `graph.attests` output rows directly (never re-implementing the adapter's own containment algorithm a second time), which is the discipline that makes this a genuine independent check rather than a tautology.
files.l3: `spoken_at_coverage_over_the_real_data_is_461_of_470_pinned` (94) pins `graph.spoken_by.len() == 470`, all distinct, and `graph.spoken_at`'s distinct covered-range count at exactly 461 (9 uncovered). `every_uncovered_range_is_assessed_and_is_a_genuine_data_gap_not_a_predicate_bug` (128) categorizes each of the 9 as either 'too-narrow' (a located event's reconstructed span overlaps the range but doesn't fully contain it — needs new Attests rows, a data change) or 'disconnected' (no located event's span overlaps at all — needs a located event that doesn't exist in the source data), printing each range's category and asserting the split totals 9. Disposition: DOCUMENT-ONLY per RED-m2's own ticket — `data/` stays byte-untouched, no code fix is available without new source location data landing first.

files.role: The M-B acceptance centerpiece: the graph's own event ordering must equal the pre-graph resolver's ordering exactly.
files.l1: Before this app used a graph for everything, it had an older way of figuring out which Bible event came before which. This test proves the new, graph-based ordering produces the identical sequence of events as the old one did — a single, decisive proof that switching to the graph didn't quietly re-shuffle anyone's timeline.
files.l2: Compares two independently-computed total orders over the same real data: the OLD order, walked via `AtlasData::timeline_event_at(i)` in a `while let Some(...) = ...` loop (Rust's 'keep going while this pattern matches' construct) until it returns `None`; the NEW order, built by re-resolving every real `graph.dated_by` row's stored placement via `event_world::resolve_timepoint` (never trusting a cached value) into a `HashMap<String, ResolvedPlacement>`, then `sort_by`'d using `temporal_order`. Deliberately calls the OLD resolver's own public accessor rather than reading `AtlasData.events` directly, so this test can't accidentally reimplement (and silently diverge from) the very algorithm it's checking.
files.l3: `the_graphs_total_order_over_resolved_placements_equals_the_old_resolvers_timeline_order_exactly` (63) asserts `ew_stats.dated_events >= 450` and `graph.dated_by.len() == ew_stats.dated_events` (one DatedBy row per dated event), independently re-resolves every row and cross-checks the recovered year against `atlas.event_by_id(...).when.from_year`, then does `graph_order.sort_by(|a,b| temporal_order(&resolved[a], &resolved[b]))` and asserts `graph_order == old_order` element-for-element — 'THE ACCEPTANCE CENTERPIECE' per the assertion's own message. A closing loop constructs `EventId::new(id.clone())` for every id in the old order as a second witness that no id-encoding bug could make a garbled-but-consistent comparison silently pass.

files.role: Pins the graph's content-hash version root to an exact value, with a full changelog of every deliberate move.
files.l1: The whole graph has a single fingerprint (a content hash) that changes if, and only if, its actual content changes. This test pins that fingerprint to one exact value over the real data — and every time a real, deliberate change to the atlas's content lands, the pinned value is updated in that same commit with a one-line reason. The huge comment block at the bottom of this file is effectively a changelog of every real content change the atlas has ever made, in order.
files.l2: The test itself is short: build the real graph (eras-less, via `GraphService::from_sources_with_eras_and_brainfuel_and_concord_and_kretzmann`), compute its hex-rendered version via `atlas_graph::version_hex(svc.snapshot().version())`, and `assert_eq!` it against a single `const EXPECTED_VERSION_HEX`. The interesting content is the huge trailing comment: roughly 30 numbered 'MOVED (deliberately -- ...)' entries, each naming the batch, what content changed, and the new hex value — a real audit trail proving 'content addressing is your regression harness' (design doc §9b) in practice, not just in theory.
files.l3: `version_root_matches_the_captured_pre_pipeline_baseline` (52) threads real brainfuel/Concord/Kretzmann data through the build so the root reflects the same graph `atlas-graph-compile` actually ships (minus eras, a disclosed, historical difference from the compile binary's own with-eras root). The current pinned value is `EXPECTED_VERSION_HEX = "59c6f7dc236f6f23"` (line 371), following the ATTEST-1 batch's changes (one new Event node `mat_leper_healed`, two changed Event payloads). The comment history documents every prior move back to the pre-pipeline baseline `4ad17fd0f68660f7`, each tied to a specific adapter/data change (new adapters, payload widenings, event merges, KJV-case restoration, new corpora, PeopleGroup reclassification, and more) — useful as a map of the crate's whole content-evolution history, not just a hash log.

files.role: Property-based proof that reading windows compose correctly, over both the port and the raw graph.
files.l1: The reader loads the Bible in small chunks (a 'window' of verses) as you scroll, rather than all 31,000+ verses at once. This test proves that however you slice up your reading into windows — one big chunk, or many small ones — you always get exactly the same text back, in the same order. That's what guarantees lazy loading can never quietly change what the Bible says.
files.l2: Uses `proptest`, a property-based testing library: instead of hand-picking example inputs, each `#[test]` inside the `proptest! { ... }` macro block runs many randomly-generated inputs (here, random start positions and random window-size partitions) and checks a general rule holds for all of them, catching edge cases a human wouldn't think to write by hand. `prop_assume!` discards a randomly generated case that wouldn't make sense (e.g. a partition that would run off the end of the Bible) rather than treating it as a failure. The graph is accessed only through `&dyn GraphQuery` — a Rust *trait object* (a value manipulated only through its trait's methods, its concrete type erased) — proving the window law holds at the same abstract seam any future storage backend would plug into, not just for one concrete implementation.
files.l3: `partition_concatenation_matches_the_single_whole_window` (69) generates a random start fraction and a `Vec<usize>` of 1-12 window sizes (1-50 each), computes one 'whole' window and a manually-concatenated sequence of per-piece windows, and asserts they're identical — proving `window::window`'s core algebraic law: partitioning is invariant under concatenation. `backward_window_is_the_mirror_of_an_onward_one` (98) proves a `WindowDir::Backward` window ending at a position equals the `WindowDir::Onward` window starting where it starts. `holds_against_the_raw_graph_too_not_just_a_snapshot` (120) re-runs the law against `real_raw_graph()` (a raw `graph_types::graph::Graph`, graph-types' own canonical `GraphQuery` instance) rather than a `MemSnapshot`, proving the window functions are generically correct, not merely working by coincidence against one implementation. `bible_len()` (48) is cached in a `OnceLock` since `GraphQuery` deliberately has no dedicated 'spine length' operation — computing it means walking the whole corpus once.
